evidence_candidates.claim: The crosswalk identifies a supply-chain attestation gap: AIUC-1 covers vendor due diligence and change approvals, but does not require tool manifests, prompt version control, agent dependency bills of materials, code signing for agents and tools, or structured schemas at the agent-model boundary.
evidence_candidates.relevance: Directly informs third-party assurance, component inventory, change control, signing, and runtime supply-chain governance.

evidence_candidates.claim: AIUC-1 B001 is described as an adversarial testing program to validate resilience against adversarial inputs and prompt-injection attempts.
evidence_candidates.relevance: Candidate assurance control for independent security testing of AI systems and connected components.

evidence_candidates.claim: AIUC-1 C010 and C011 describe appointing expert third parties at least every three months to evaluate harmful outputs and out-of-scope outputs, respectively.
evidence_candidates.relevance: Supports a candidate for independent recurring testing and third-party assurance; frequency remains source guidance, not a binding rule.

evidence_candidates.claim: The crosswalk describes D003 as restricting unsafe tool calls so that AI systems cannot execute unauthorized actions, access restricted information, or act beyond intended scope; it also notes that authorization may need revalidation at execution time in distributed or asynchronous workflows.
evidence_candidates.relevance: Directly supports tool permission boundaries, delegated authority checks, and third-party tool invocation governance.

evidence_candidates.claim: The crosswalk describes E005 as establishing criteria for cloud versus on-premises processing and E006 as establishing AI vendor due-diligence processes for foundation and upstream model providers; E007 covers documented system change approvals and approval records.
evidence_candidates.relevance: Candidate third-party onboarding, hosting selection, change-control, and upstream-provider assurance controls.

evidence_candidates.claim: The crosswalk describes E009 as implementing systems to monitor third-party access, with mappings to tool misuse, identity and privilege abuse, agentic supply-chain vulnerabilities, insecure inter-agent communication, and human-agent trust exploitation.
evidence_candidates.relevance: Candidate monitoring and auditability control for vendors, external tools, and connected services.

evidence_candidates.claim: The described ANSSI lifecycle highlights access to data sources, libraries, and internal and external services as attack targets during an AI system project lifecycle.
evidence_candidates.relevance: Establishes that third-party libraries and services are part of the AI attack surface across lifecycle stages.

evidence_candidates.claim: The report defines supply-chain attacks as modification or replacement of libraries, models, associated data, or deployment platforms used by an AI system, and describes downstream risks including biased results, security flaws, and system outages.
evidence_candidates.relevance: Supports the scope of AI third-party and dependency risk.

evidence_candidates.claim: The report presents ANSSI recommendations to assess the trustworthiness of external libraries and external data sources used by an AI system.
evidence_candidates.relevance: Candidate baseline for external-component trust assessment, deployment assurance, integration controls, and third-party permission review.

evidence_candidates.claim: The report's comparison table links identifying and protecting AI components, AI BOM maintenance, and dataset-source and modification-history provenance to supply-chain risk reduction and vulnerability response.
evidence_candidates.relevance: Candidate component inventory, AIBOM, provenance, and vulnerability-response controls.

evidence_candidates.claim: The report's checklist calls for protecting AI files' integrity, verifying cryptographic checksums of AI artifacts, and assessing trust in libraries and external modules.
evidence_candidates.relevance: Candidate integrity, external-component trust, provenance, and telemetry controls for third-party supply chains.

evidence_candidates.claim: The report states that AI systems inherit third-party software supply-chain risks through frameworks, libraries, orchestration layers, and cloud services, and that AIBOM practices extend inventory to model versions, providers, training lineage where available, and runtime environments.
evidence_candidates.relevance: Defines the third-party component and provenance scope for AI supply-chain governance.

evidence_candidates.claim: The report says that agentic supply-chain governance must inventory models, datasets, RAG, MCP servers, agent frameworks, connectors, tool ecosystems, and external registries, and extend governance to runtime composition, delegated agents, and external context sources.
evidence_candidates.relevance: Directly supports an authoritative third-party and runtime component inventory and supply-chain scope.

evidence_candidates.claim: The adoption-tier model distinguishes vendor-embedded and platform-integrated agents from externally extended agents using MCP servers, plugins, or third-party APIs, and from federated agents operating across organizational boundaries.
evidence_candidates.relevance: Provides a bounded way to classify third-party trust boundaries and escalating supply-chain exposure.

evidence_candidates.claim: The report describes a delegated-access compromise pattern in which employees authorize third-party AI tools with broad OAuth scopes, allowing a later compromise of the vendor to operate inside the trust boundary using legitimately granted access.
evidence_candidates.relevance: Supports third-party access scoping, OAuth governance, non-human identity review, and vendor compromise scenarios.

evidence_candidates.claim: The report identifies managed connectors, external tools, source repositories, CI/CD pipelines, cloud infrastructure, package registries, developer credentials, customer data, payment processors, and backend APIs as trust-boundary exposures for enterprise, coding, and client-facing agents.
evidence_candidates.relevance: Maps external services, tools, data, and credentials that require third-party security review.

evidence_candidates.claim: The report states that a compromised commit or poisoned dependency used by a coding agent can propagate automatically through downstream projects, amplifying impact beyond the initially targeted codebase.
evidence_candidates.relevance: Supports transitive-dependency and downstream propagation risk in third-party AI tooling.

evidence_candidates.claim: The report's regulatory overview attributes supply-chain and third-party-provider implications to DORA and NIS2, including oversight of critical ICT providers and runtime third-party tools and services; these legal characterizations require separate legal-source audit before use as obligations.
evidence_candidates.relevance: Flags potential legal and third-party oversight intersections while preserving the non-authoritative status of this report.

evidence_candidates.claim: The report describes DHS guidance as covering AI supply-chain risk management and minimum security requirements for AI vendors and third-party developers in critical infrastructure, while describing NIST AI 600-1 as voluntary guidance covering third-party model integration and value-chain risk.
evidence_candidates.relevance: Candidate framework references for vendor assurance and supply-chain risk; authority and currentness require review.

evidence_candidates.claim: The report summarizes voluntary security frameworks that address agent zero trust, mutual authentication, model signing and attestation, MCP threats, inter-agent identity, and supply-chain integrity across model artifacts, training data, and runtime components.
evidence_candidates.relevance: Supports cross-reference candidates for MCP, identity, attestation, and runtime supply-chain controls.

evidence_candidates.claim: The report summarizes ISO/IEC 42001 as a third-party-auditable AI management-system standard whose supply-chain governance covers full agent dependency chains and procurement and vendor management for model providers, tool vendors, and orchestration platforms.
evidence_candidates.relevance: Candidate source for third-party assurance and procurement governance; the report summary is not binding evidence of the standard's requirements.

evidence_candidates.claim: The report describes a shared-responsibility and control-inheritance model in which organizations may inherit compliance controls from cloud and AI model providers, while noting that agentic deployments invoke tools and models from multiple providers.
evidence_candidates.relevance: Directly informs shared responsibility, evidence inheritance, and residual accountability across multi-vendor deployments.

evidence_candidates.claim: For externally extended and federated agents, the report identifies supply-chain verification, MCP authentication, agent-to-agent identity, tool-scope verification, third-party risk assessment, behavioral monitoring, mutual attestation, federated identity, cross-organization governance SLAs, and tamper-evident audit trails as primary mitigations.
evidence_candidates.relevance: Candidate control set for external tools, cross-organization trust, identity, assurance, and exit or incident evidence planning.

evidence_candidates.claim: The report lists recommendations to secure interactions between an AI system and other business applications, limit automatic actions from systems processing uncontrolled inputs, log all processing performed within the AI system, and regularly review the permissions configuration of third-party generative-AI tools used with business applications.
evidence_candidates.relevance: Candidate integration, action-gating, logging, and third-party permission-review controls.

evidence_candidates.claim: The report's checklist calls for maintaining dataset provenance, logging AI model inputs and outputs, and protecting training data integrity.
evidence_candidates.relevance: Candidate provenance and telemetry controls for externally sourced data and services.

evidence_candidates.claim: The adoption-tier model defines externally extended agents as connecting to external tools or services across trust boundaries and federated agents as operating across organizational boundaries, including cross-organization supply-chain agents and multi-tenant marketplaces.
evidence_candidates.relevance: Directly supports cross-boundary third-party and concentration-risk scoping.

evidence_candidates.claim: The report describes client-facing agents as publicly accessible systems connected to customer data, payment processors, scheduling, CRM, and backend APIs, with managed connectors identified as a supply-chain exposure.
evidence_candidates.relevance: Candidate external-service inventory and third-party impact scoping for customer-facing agents.

evidence_candidates.claim: The report's NIS2 summary states that its supply-chain-security discussion covers third-party tools and services that agents access at runtime; this is a report summary requiring primary-source legal verification.
evidence_candidates.relevance: Flags a potential runtime third-party control intersection without creating an obligation.

evidence_candidates.claim: The report characterizes NIST AI 600-1 as voluntary guidance whose value-chain and component-integration discussion covers third-party model integration, fine-tuning risks, and downstream deployment scenarios.
evidence_candidates.relevance: Candidate non-binding reference for third-party model integration review.

evidence_candidates.claim: For multi-agent and federated deployments, the report lists supply-chain verification, MCP authentication, agent-to-agent identity, tool-scope verification, third-party risk assessment, behavioral monitoring, mutual attestation, federated identity, cross-organization governance SLAs, and tamper-evident audit trails as primary mitigations.
evidence_candidates.relevance: Candidate controls for cross-organizational trust, third-party assurance, runtime identity, and evidence continuity.

evidence_candidates.locator: Sheet mitigations, cells A1:H40; row 15 (AML.M0013 Code Signing)
evidence_candidates.claim: The MITRE ATLAS mitigation describes digital-signature verification for binaries and applications and recommends cryptographic signing of SBOM and AIBOM components to protect AI supply-chain integrity.
evidence_candidates.relevance: Candidate artifact integrity and provenance control for third-party components.

evidence_candidates.locator: Sheet mitigations, cells A1:H40; rows 18, 25-30 (selected MITRE mitigations)
evidence_candidates.claim: The selected mitigation rows describe scanning model artifacts and external dependencies, maintaining AI BOM and dataset provenance, logging AI agent activity and tool use, and applying least-privilege and delegated-access controls to privileged agents and shared tools.
evidence_candidates.relevance: Candidate control bundle for dependency assurance, inventory, provenance, monitoring, and tool permissions.

evidence_candidates.locator: Sheet techniques addressed, cells A1:M250; rows 155-157, 232, 248
evidence_candidates.claim: The MITRE relationship rows associate artifact and tool-registry scanning with poisoned AI artifacts and AI agent tools, associate AI BOMs with identifying untrustworthy supply-chain components, and associate tool-invocation logging with detecting malicious calls.
evidence_candidates.relevance: Provides structured technique-to-mitigation links for supply-chain scanning, AIBOM, and telemetry.

evidence_candidates.locator: Sheet techniques addressed, cells A251:M347; rows 305-309, 328, 337
evidence_candidates.claim: The relationship rows describe controlled tests of untrusted software, datasets, models, and agent tools and call for verifying source authorization, provenance, scanning, signing, review, permission boundaries, safe activation, tool-call controls, change approval, integrity monitoring, and restoration from trusted configurations.
evidence_candidates.relevance: Candidate third-party acquisition, testing, activation, permission, and rollback controls.

evidence_candidates.claim: MITRE ATLAS identifies AI agent tools as a distinct AI supply-chain target because connected services, data sources, and execution capabilities may provide broad access and permissions.
evidence_candidates.relevance: Directly supports third-party tool and connector risk assessment.

evidence_candidates.claim: MITRE ATLAS describes a poisoned AI agent tool as capable of altering definitions or runtime responses, invoking additional tools, executing malicious logic, or creating unauthorized access.
evidence_candidates.relevance: Candidate threat scenario for tool-provider review, runtime integrity, and permission containment.

evidence_candidates.claim: MITRE ATLAS includes mitigations for AI dataset provenance, input and output validation, authority expansion controls, and detection of drift from an agent's authorized scope.
evidence_candidates.relevance: Candidate controls for third-party data lineage, runtime validation, authority boundaries, and scope monitoring.
